请使用 OpenSCAD 设计一个适合 FDM 3D 打印的双翼可活动蝴蝶模型，要求采用一体化3D打印结构。模型由 1 个固定躯干和左右 2 片独立活动翅膀组成，共 3 个独立刚体零件。蝴蝶应具有可辨识的头部、躯干、左右对称的翅膀造型，可添加翅膀纹理及装饰，但不能影响运动。中立姿态下整体外接尺寸不得超过 120 × 100 × 30 mm（X × Y × Z）。以 X 轴为躯干纵向、Y 轴为左右翅膀展开方向、Z 轴为竖直方向。
结构要求：1.左右翅膀分别通过一个独立的销轴式旋转关节连接到固定躯干，共 2 个旋转关节。2.两个关节的旋转轴均平行于 Z 轴，使左右翅膀能够在 XY 平面内摆动。3.每片翅膀相对于中立位置均须能够向两个方向各旋转至少 30°，即运动范围覆盖 -30° 至 +30°。4.左右翅膀应能够独立运动。一侧翅膀转动时，另一侧可以保持静止。5.当左右翅膀同时在规定角度范围内运动时，两片翅膀及躯干之间不得发生不允许的几何干涉。6.两个关节均需设置轴向防脱结构，避免翅膀沿关节轴线直接脱出。
3d打印条件与要求限制：1.使用PLA材料、0.4mm 喷嘴、0.2mm 层高。2.旋转轴与轴孔的单侧径向设计间隙为0.4–0.6mm。3.关节其他相邻活动面也应留有明确的非零间隙，避免零件在打印中融合。4.所有零件必须在装配状态下一次打印完成，不允许后期安装销轴、螺丝或其他零件。5.关节活动间隙内不得依赖支撑材料。
交付要求：1.model.scad：完整参数化源代码。2.model.stl：中立姿态下的完整模型。3.parts/*.stl：3 个零件（躯干、左翅、右翅）的独立 STL，用于验证运动，用序号命名，例如 parts_1.stl。4.joints.json：声明固定躯干、左右翅膀、两个关节的旋转轴、位置和预期运动范围，以支持独立运动验证。5.说明打印方向及实际完成的几何与切片检查。

【文件与环境】
- 交付文件都写到 `/app/output/`：`model.scad`、`model.stl`、`joints.json` 直接放在 `/app/output/` 下；各零件的独立 STL 放在 `/app/output/parts/` 下，每个文件一个零件，用序号命名（`parts_1.stl`、`parts_2.stl`……）。打印方向和检查说明等其他文件也放在 `/app/output/` 下。
- STL 单位为 mm。`parts/` 下的零件与 `model.stl` 使用同一坐标系和同一姿态，所有零件合在一起就是 `model.stl`。
- 可用工具：Python 3（numpy、scipy、trimesh、manifold3d、shapely、cadquery、matplotlib、vtk）、OpenSCAD（`openscad`）、`xvfb-run`，以及 PrusaSlicer 命令行（`prusa-slicer`）。`/opt/slicer/` 里有按 0.4 mm 喷嘴、0.2 mm 层高、PLA 准备的切片配置（基于 Bambu Lab P1S），用法见 `/opt/slicer/README.md`。
- 没有互联网，也没有显示器。

You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gemini-4-argon-high model.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Read an existing file before overwriting it with write (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Read a file before editing it (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

Use the workflow tool ONLY when the user explicitly asks for a workflow or for large multi-agent orchestration: you write a JavaScript script (the tool description documents the exact format) that fans work out across many subagents with phases and structured results. For one or two delegations, prefer plain subagent calls.

Start independent subagent delegations together in one assistant message and continue useful work while they run.

Your working directory is /app.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Managed `$DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Before any delete or move, verify that the resolved absolute target path is the intended one; never run it against a computed path you have not checked. An unset variable expands to an empty string, so guard variables in such paths with `${VAR:?}`. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact command the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create a persisted goal that keeps this session working across automatic continuation rounds. Use it when the direct human request is a long-running objective, even if the user did not say "goal"; not for single-turn work.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact operation the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current session goal, including the id and revision that update_goal requires.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files, not directories, whose paths match a glob pattern, including hidden and ignored files. Returns up to 100 paths in modification-time order; a larger result keeps the first paths and reports where the complete list was saved.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns up to 250 matches; a larger result reports where the complete match list was saved.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Ask a subagent to stop its current work. This call returns without waiting for it to stop. You can continue a direct child's conversation later with send_message. Subagents it started will keep running.

agent_id.description: The id of an agent created under you: your direct child or a deeper descendant.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job: output since the previous read for stream jobs, or the result of a finished final-output job.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job finishes or the timeout expires; a timed-out wait leaves the job running. Defaults to false.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds with wait: true. Defaults to and is capped by configuration.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List subagents you started, with their ids, labels, and status. running means it is working; inactive means it is not currently working. You will be notified when a subagent finishes; there is no need to keep checking its status. Use send_message to continue the conversation.

scope.description: children (default) lists direct children, which accept send_message in any status. descendants lists the whole tree below you with each entry's parent session id and depth; entries deeper than 1 accept only interrupt_agent.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. Large images are downscaled automatically; do not install image libraries or create thumbnails to inspect an image.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an agent. A working agent receives it at its next step; an idle agent starts a new turn with it. Returns delivery confirmation, not the agent's answer.

agent_id.description: The agent id of your direct continuable child, or your direct parent when you are a resident continuable child.

message.description: The message to deliver to the agent.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for a skill. Call it before acting on a task that names or clearly matches a skill in the session skill catalog.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. It runs in the background by default and returns a subagent id you can continue with `send_message`; you are notified when the run settles.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task for the subagent. It does not share this conversation's context, so include everything it needs.

run_in_background.description: Defaults to true. Set false only when your next action depends on the result.

tools.name: subagent_fork
tools.description: Delegate a task to a subagent that inherits this conversation: a child agent seeded with all completed turns so far (it does not see the current in-flight turn). Use this when the subtask builds on this conversation's context — a follow-up analysis, a review, a continuation — without consuming this conversation's context for the work itself. You receive its result, not its intermediate steps. This call waits for the result by default.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The task for the subagent. It already sees this conversation's completed turns, so build on them freely and state only what is new.

run_in_background.description: Run as a background job and return its id (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). Defaults to false.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a task list to plan multi-step work and show progress; skip it for trivial single-step tasks. Add one todo per concrete step before you start. While work remains, keep the todos being worked on `in_progress`, several only when work runs in parallel. Mark each todo `completed` as soon as it is done.

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the current goal.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

action.description: edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. complete and blocked are also allowed during an automatic continuation of this goal; blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Required only with action blocked: the concrete condition that persisted across rounds and blocks progress.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

script.description: The plain JavaScript body, not TypeScript and without an `export const meta` statement; top-level await is allowed. End with `return <value>`; the JSON-serializable value is this tool's result.

meta.description: The workflow identity as plain JSON, not code.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

run_in_background.description: Run as a background job: return a job id immediately instead of waiting; the return value arrives with the completion notice.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

sandbox_permissions.description: The narrowest wider sandbox mode for a one-shot retry of the exact operation the sandbox just denied; the retry asks the user for approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access. Use the language of the user’s current request.

- 交付文件都写到 `/app/output/`：`model.scad`、`model.stl`、`joints.json` 直接放在 `/app/output/` 下；各零件的独立 STL 放在 `/app/output/parts/` 下，每个文件一个零件，用序号命名（`parts_1.stl`、`parts_2.stl`……）。打印方向和检查说明等其他文件也放在 `/app/output/` 下。
- STL 单位为 mm。`parts/` 下的零件与 `model.stl` 使用同一坐标系和同一姿态，所有零件合在一起就是 `model.stl`。
- 可用工具：Python 3（numpy、scipy、trimesh、manifold3d、shapely、cadquery、matplotlib、vtk）、OpenSCAD（`openscad`）、`xvfb-run`，以及 PrusaSlicer 命令行（`prusa-slicer`）。`/opt/slicer/` 里有按 0.4 mm 喷嘴、0.2 mm 层高、PLA 准备的切片配置（基于 Bambu Lab P1S），用法见 `/opt/slicer/README.md`。
- 没有互联网，也没有显示器。

Proper part separation is crucial; the final model file must be the union of these three distinct components.

The bounding box limits are critically important; the design must stay within 120x100x30mm, requiring close verification during part creation and assembly. A preliminary target size of ~86x94x12mm will ensure compliance.


Two pin-type revolute joints are required, one for each wing, with rotation about the Z-axis in the XY plane. Each wing's range of motion must be at least +/-30 degrees, with additional mechanical clearance for safety, allowing independent movement.  Ensuring well-proportioned features throughout rotation is crucial.


Each wing joint must be independently functional and avoid collisions during rotation within the specified range. Axial retention along the Z-axis requires a print-in-place mechanism, posing a design challenge. Consideration is turning to classic FDM hinge mechanisms, particularly those with axial retention like captured double-clevis designs, focusing on how to make a Z-axis pin captive.


Examining a captured middle knuckle design (3-lug clevis hinge) to retain a vertical pin axially during print-in-place. Considering the Torso having bottom and top lugs with the wing's knuckle barrel in between, or vice versa, to trace overhangs during printing. Investigating a conical/biconical vertical-axis hinge (or 45° chamfered pin/collar) as an alternative.


Anchoring both the Torso and Wings flat on the build plate (Z=0) maximizes first-layer bed adhesion, critical for FDM printing. This eliminates the need for supports under either the Torso or Wing. The joint will be a pin-and-hole revolute type with a radial clearance of approximately 0.45mm.


Analyzing joint geometry in the radial-vertical plane to ensure print-in-place functionality and compliance with design constraints. texts:
Defining the coordinate system is the first step, establishing the X-axis as a primary reference. Need to ensure the model adheres to all geometric, kinematic, printability (FDM), and aesthetic constraints.


Establishing a right-handed coordinate system, defining +X as the butterfly's head (anterior) and -X as the abdomen (posterior). Defining the Y-axis as the wingspan (+Y left wing, -Y right wing), ensuring symmetry across the XZ plane.

Setting the Z-axis as the vertical print direction, with the model's base at Z = 0. Ensuring the model dimensions are within the 120x100x30 mm bounding box by targeting X~86mm, Y~92mm, and Z~14mm.


Considering wing rotation of ±30°, verifying that the neutral pose dimensions (86x92x14 mm) remain within the bounding box of 120x100x30 mm. Assessing aspect ratio by modeling the butterfly's dimensions as X (body length) and Y (wingspan) against the specified limit. The target size is Y~94mm and X~84-96mm.


Joint rotation axis will be parallel to the Z-axis, enabling wing movement in the XY plane, requiring precise joint center coordinates. Considering joint centers at X_joint = +8.0 mm, Y_joint = ±10.0 mm (or ±6.0mm), the Y_joint value needs careful evaluation for its impact on torso width, pin dimensions, and rotation clearance.

Analyzing the pin-in-hole structure with axial retention, the design clearance between the rotation shaft and shaft hole must be maintained within the 0.4-0.6 mm range.


Considering design constraints: Adjacent moving surfaces need clearance, axial retention is required, print-in-place is mandatory, and no support material within joint clearance. Architecture A (Captured Diabolo/Double-Cone Pin) will be compared to another approach, focusing on its ability to satisfy these constraints. The objective is a robust, support-free, 0.5 mm radial clearance pin joint with axial retention.


Every independent part must have a flat base on the build plate (Z=0) for support-free print-in-place FDM. If the Torso, Left Wing, and Right Wing are all on Z=0, no parts float. The challenge arises if both wing and torso are on Z=0; how does the pin connect them at the joint center?


Analyzing joint design Option 1: a pin anchored to the torso (Z=0 to H_joint) with an enlarged head or collar, and a wing with a bore around the pin. This creates a potential overhang if a bottom arm is added to the torso at Z=0..2.4mm, forcing the wing hub to float at Z=2.8mm to avoid collision.

Investigating alternative designs to eliminate internal overhangs and ensure both pin and wing base rest on Z=0. The challenge becomes how to connect them at the joint.

Realized the wing blade outside the hub can indeed rest on Z=0, simplifying the problem. The core issue remains: How to have the wing and pin bases both on Z=0.


Considering different joint configurations:  Torso-based pin with wing bore, or vice-versa.  Re-examining the prompt to ensure adherence to clearance and anti-detachment requirements. The objective is to evaluate each pin-and-bore geometry's feasibility for Z=0 base-flat printability.


Focusing on the radial cross-section, the design must incorporate a cylindrical pin and bore with specified radial clearance. Axial retention in both directions, without horizontal overhangs within the joint, is critical. The pin and bore must connect to the torso and wing respectively, both resting flat at Z=0.

Analyzing whether a pin-in-bore configuration can satisfy the zero-overhang requirement while allowing both parts to be Z=0 flat. The challenge is in achieving both axial retention and printability. A solution must prevent the wing from disengaging in the Z+ and Z- directions.


Considering topological constraints, if the bore surrounds the pin fully, the wing can connect outward, but the pin's inward connection is limited. The pin must transition through a region without the bore.

Method 1 involves an axial bridge or conical transition; if the pin connects to the torso at the top or bottom, the bore can only exist within a limited Z range, potentially leading to a shorter connecting section.


Examining support for the Wing's Bore, considering a 45-degree conical slope. Realized the inner ring of the bore at a specific Z-height is a Z-minimum unless connected to the Wing at Z=0.

Considering Method 2, hypothesizing the Pin and Bore could originate at Z=0. Questioning the feasibility of both starting at the build plate.


Analyzing several pin-torso connection methods: a 45-degree conical arm, an angular opening, and a 360-degree bore with top/bottom connections. These configurations require mathematical analysis to determine feasibility.
A ring around a pin with z > 0 creates a floating local minimum because the ring is offset from the base build plate Z=0.


The core challenge is ensuring the pin and wing hub, both originating at Z=0, can connect. Considering the pin's base at Z=0, and a bore surrounding it at Z=0, it's feasible to connect the wing hub to the bore. The pin could connect to the torso through a neck at Z=0. Questioning whether a full 360-degree bore extending from Z=0 is printable, or if a partial bore is needed for printability.


Considering a pin-in-bore connection and the constraint of both parts resting at Z=0, a connection to the torso solely at the top, above a certain z-height, is under consideration. The pin, originating from Z=0, is fully supported, with an overhang connecting it to the torso. Axial retention at the pin's base at Z=0 raises a concern. The pin needs a way to connect to the torso, and an axial restriction is needed at the bottom.


A flared pin base at Z=0 is being considered as a possible solution. Examining a top-connected pin with a flared base, the design is being traced layer by layer from Z=0 to Z=H.

At Z=0, the torso body, the pin's base (part of the torso), and the wing's joint hub all sit directly on the build plate. The pin base radius at Z=0 is R_cap (4.2 mm), and the wing's inner hole radius at Z=0 is R_cap + clearance (4.7 mm).

As Z increases from 0 up to z_1, the pin tapers inwards from radius R_cap to the cylindrical shaft radius R_pin (2.6 mm).


From Z=0 to Z=3.0 mm, the pin tapers inwards, achieving a zero-overhang configuration. The wing's bore also tapers inwards, starting from a radius of 4.7mm at Z=0 to 3.1mm at Z=3.0 mm, with a constant slope. This inward taper allows for printability.

From Z=3.0 to Z=8.0 mm, the pin becomes a vertical cylinder with a constant radius of 2.6mm. This section provides the journal bearing functionality within the pin-in-bore assembly.


The cylindrical section of the pin and bore establish the 0.5 mm radial clearance, ensuring smooth rotation. The pin's outward flare from Z=8.0 mm to Z=10.0 mm provides top axial retention, offering a printable, self-supporting overhang. The wing bore also flares outward in this region.


Examining the implications of a single pin part, connected to the torso, extending upwards through the wing hub.  Considering a pin-torso connection at Z > 10.0 mm creates a gap between torso and pin which the wing hub passes through. Questioning if a pin that wraps *around* the wing at all is the right approach. Exploring connecting the pin to the torso at *both* the bottom and top to simplify the design.

Coordinate system definition requires careful consideration. The X-axis will align with the insect's torso, with the tail at the negative end and the head at the positive. The Y-axis will be aligned with the wing span. This establishes the fundamental spatial framework.


The coordinate system and size constraints must be defined, considering the physical printing limits and realistic insect proportions. Preliminary calculations suggest an X-dimension of 88mm, Y-dimension of 92mm, and Z-dimension of 12-15mm to stay well within the print bed's bounding box. Print-in-place revolute joints with axial retention along the Z-axis appear appropriate for wing articulation.


Considering a Z-axis pin joint with axial retention, the design requires two revolute joints, each allowing ±30° rotation in the XY plane, with axial retention to prevent disengagement.  A 0.4-0.6 mm radial clearance between the pin and bore, and non-zero gaps between all moving surfaces is crucial, with no reliance on support material in the joint's active region.
Examining a captive clevis/double-lug torso bracket combined with a wing knuckle using a cylindrical pin with conical or flanged axial retention (or a fixed captive pin in the torso) seems like a promising approach.


Considering two possible pin placement scenarios, either the pin is part of the torso or the wing knuckle, with the other part having the bore. If the pin is on the torso, the base and top of the pin require specific Z-axis dimensions, extending from Z=0 to 2.4mm and Z=9.6mm to 12.0mm.

The design mandates a 0.4-0.6 mm radial clearance between the pin and bore. Ensure a cylindrical pin and a matching cylindrical bore are modeled with radii $R_{pin}$ and $R_{bore}$ to satisfy this clearance requirement.


The wing and torso must each have a stable base on the print bed (Z=0) for support. This necessitates a print-in-place design that integrates axial retention while both parts rest on the build plate. The challenge is connecting the torso and wing at Z=0 and achieving axial retention along the Z-axis.


The pin, centered at (X_joint, ±Y_joint), must connect to either the torso or the wing. A direct connection might be problematic given the surrounding nature of the joint; therefore, it requires additional structural members.

Specifically, the Torso Arm/Bridge will connect the torso to the pin (or housing) and the Wing Root will connect the wing to the housing (or pin). Considering an alternative joint design, the Housing could fully wrap the pin at certain Z-levels, and the pin can connect to its parent through a sector slot, or other axial restraint mechanism. This also opens the possibility of using a clevis/yoke joint or a captive conical-collar pin joint.


Architecture 1 features a vertical pin on the torso, connected via a base and inboard bridge, while the wing has a cylindrical bore. Starting from Z=0, both the torso and pin are directly on the build plate at the joint center. A solid neck connects the torso body to the pin from Z=0 to Z=12mm.


Considering a clevis/fork design where the torso has lower and upper lugs connected by a pin, the focus shifts to the region between the lugs (Z = 2.4 to 9.6 mm). A wing knuckle, wrapping the pin from Z = 3.0 to 9.0 mm, presents a challenge at Z = 0 due to potential overhang. This overhang could be mitigated by a conical transition or by the wing knuckle also sitting flat at Z = 0.


Analyzing how both the pin and housing can be flat at Z=0 while providing 360-degree enclosure and axial retention. The design, termed "Print-in-Place Captive Stepped/Conical Pin Joint", requires examination of its cross-section in the (r, Z) plane. Focusing on the wing bore housing, which also rests flat on the build plate from Z=0 to 12mm, with an outer radius of 6.5mm. Determining the inner profile, given these constraints, is the next step.

Considering the butterfly design holistically, aim for robust mechanical function across all axes of movement, while also ensuring aesthetic fidelity to the insect. Evaluate if the dimensions provide adequate space for internal mechanisms and external features to be both printable and visually appealing.

Initial focus is on meticulously designing the butterfly model to meet all requirements: mechanical function, movement, 3D printing feasibility, and visual appeal. The first step involves establishing a coordinate system and defining overall dimensions.


Defined a 3D coordinate system to frame the butterfly model, specifying X (torso), Y (wingspan), and Z (vertical) axes within defined dimensional constraints. The Z-axis clarifies that both the torso and wing bases should ideally rest on the build plate. Considering print-in-place feasibility, it's essential to ensure all parts have secure bed adhesion, particularly at joints.


Z = 0 is a critical condition; if both torso and wings contact the build plate at Z = 0, Layer 1 prints base features on the plate. Axial retention and print-in-place feasibility for a Z-axis pin joint are achievable when parts touch Z=0.


A Z-axis pin joint with the required clearances and axial retention needs careful design for print-in-place feasibility. The wing joint design must incorporate a mechanism preventing axial disengagement, such as a conical or stepped shaft/bore feature, ensuring parts remain captive during motion. The 0.5mm radial clearance necessitates precise feature design, factoring in potential print resolution limitations to prevent part fusion and motion restriction.


Analyzing joint design to determine which part contains the pin and which the sleeve; focusing on a Z-axis joint at (6.0, ±10.0). Considering two options: Option A places the pin on the torso with a wing-mounted sleeve, allowing the wing blade to extend to Z=0.

Option B considers a base flange on the torso; need to evaluate which design better satisfies print-in-place and motion requirements. Examining each option for print feasibility and secure bed adhesion.


Tracing Option B, if the pin is part of the torso and originates from Z=0, a support arm must reach the pin location to provide a base. The wing's knuckle encases the pin between specific Z-axis values, but the design at Z=2.4mm requires consideration: a flat overhang risks bridging a small gap, whereas a conical transition or direct contact with Z=0 offers better support and printability.


Investigating the feasibility of the wing's knuckle and torso's pin both contacting Z=0. If both touch Z=0, the pin's connection to the torso requires examination.
Considering a top bridge from the torso to connect the pin; this raises a concern. Without Z=0 support, the pin would print as an isolated feature until the top bridge is printed.
Directly supporting the pin at Z=0 offers the best support from the build plate. This would eliminate overhang during printing and connect the pin to the torso.


Considering an alternative design where the pin connects to the torso via a top arm at Z=8-10 mm; alternatively, the pin could be part of the wing, with the bore/hub on the torso, touching Z=0.

Analyzing a captive hourglass pin design with a top bridge: if the pin starts at Z=0 and connects to the torso at Z=8 mm, the pin and torso are a single, connected solid in the model.

During printing, the pin base, wing knuckle, and torso body would all start at Z=0. Evaluating if a small pin island on the print bed presents an adhesion risk before the top bridge is printed.


A full 360° enclosed bore with axial retention is under consideration, starting from the build plate (Z=0).  It's crucial to understand if the torso or wing contains the bore and how the base integrates with the build plate. The analysis focuses on ensuring no disconnected island is created during printing, especially at Z=0. The pin needs secure anchoring on the build plate.


Considering the pin's placement and the wing's base, confirming that the wing rests on Z=0 outside the torso's base (|Y| >= 14.5 mm). Examining the bore-and-pin interaction, specifically the wing's bore wrapping around the torso's pin at (X_j, ±Y_j).

Evaluating torso base height alternatives: a narrow sector or a double-shear yoke to support the pin.  Hypothesizing the roles of pin and bore: torso-bore/wing-pin versus wing-bore/torso-pin configurations, both from Z=0 to Z=9mm.


Examining axial retention methods for the wing joint, specifically the bi-directional prevention of wing sliding along the Z-axis. Considering a double-cone or hourglass profile within the pin-bore joint. Evaluating the radial clearance in a cylindrical section of the pin and bore. The calculated 0.5 mm radial clearance aligns with the specified design clearance.


Investigating how to achieve bi-directional Z-axis locking without horizontal overhangs by analyzing a flared pin and bore design.  Observed that an hourglass pin with outward flares at both ends would prevent movement in either direction within a bore with a narrower waist.  Determined that an interference issue exists because the pin's flared radius exceeds the bore's waist radius, preventing pin insertion or removal.  Thus, the current design creates a mechanical lock in the Z-axis.


Examining a revised biconical pin and bore design with cylindrical sections. Identified dimensions for a center-bulge pin and corresponding bore, considering cone angles and radii along the Z-axis. Noted an interference fit with a 1.6 mm diameter pin, or alternatively, a biconical design. Analyzing the radial and normal clearances at different Z-axis sections to determine the fit. The interference fit creates a mechanical lock, preventing Z-axis movement.


Radial clearance is precisely 0.50 mm throughout the pin-bore assembly at all Z heights. This consistent clearance is confirmed through calculations for cylindrical shaft sections and the retention ring. The conical sections' radial gap is verified based on the vertical shift.


Determining the appropriate clearance, calculations show that a 50-degree cone angle allows for a self-supporting overhang without requiring additional support structures. This angle results in specific dimensional relationships between radial and vertical gaps within the design. The pin's flared and tapered sections were verified as self-supporting due to the angles created. The bore design was evaluated similarly, confirming its self-supporting nature due to inner chamfers.
Careful design is required to ensure mechanical reliability and full adherence to specifications. The model must be easily printable without supports and possess an aesthetically pleasing appearance.

content.text:
Breaking down the design is necessary to ensure mechanical robustness and adherence to specifications. The goal is to produce a design that prints easily without supports, while also passing all relevant tests for geometry, kinematics, and slicer compatibility. Simultaneously, the design must achieve the artistic and recognizable appearance of a detailed butterfly.


Defining a coordinate system and establishing dimensional constraints is crucial for a printable and articulated butterfly model. A centered coordinate system with the X-axis representing the torso's length seems appropriate, placing the head at positive X and abdomen at negative X. The target total X-length of 96 mm stays well within the 120 mm dimension. Y-axis will represent wing span, and the model is symmetric across the XZ-plane.


Y-axis defines wing span, with the left wing at positive Y and right wing at negative Y, targeting a 92 mm total span (±46 mm). The Z-axis represents vertical height, with the model's base on the print bed at Z = 0; this means the torso and wings also rest on the build plate. This configuration ensures no unsupported overhangs during 3D printing. The maximum height is about 12 mm for the body and head, and 4-8 mm for the wings.


All model parts must rest on the print bed at Z = 0, eliminating any mid-air floating elements on the first layer. This needs careful consideration for joints requiring axial retention along the Z-axis.

A print-in-place vertical-axis pin joint can still function with parts resting at Z = 0, allowing for bidirectional axial retention. The design will now focus on the pin joint's construction and functionality to ensure both printability and axial retention.


Considering Z-axis pin joints, axial retention is crucial for print-in-place functionality. One approach uses a clevis/captive pin with a conical collar (double-cone or hourglass shape).

The other potential approach needs to be carefully investigated, considering the print-in-place constraints and axial retention requirements. Radial clearance between the pin and hole must be within 0.4-0.6 mm per side to ensure movement. All joint surfaces need non-zero gaps.


Considering a pin-type revolute joint, either the torso or the wing could contain the pin. Both configurations must be evaluated for printability. Case 1 assumes a torso-mounted captive pin and a wing-mounted bore. A pin-type joint consists of a cylindrical pin and a shaft hole with a radial clearance of 0.4-0.6 mm.


Ensuring true cylindrical sections for the pin and bore facilitates a consistent, predictable radial clearance as specified. The specified 0.4-0.6 mm single-side clearance translates directly to $c_{\text{radial}} = R_{\text{bore}} - R_{\text{pin}} = 0.50\text{ mm}$ (midpoint) in the joint cross-section.

The critical challenge now is implementing axial retention along the Z-axis without requiring any print supports or lifting parts off the build plate at Z=0. Exploring joint geometry in (r, Z) coordinates is the next step to achieve this.


The pin's connection to the torso requires careful consideration of axial retention and print-in-place constraints, specifically from Z=0 to Z=10mm. Two potential approaches are identified: a double-shear clevis pin configuration or a pin with conical retention flares. If a bottom arm supports the pin, the wing knuckle's Z-position must be evaluated to ensure proper articulation and prevent interference during printing. It's uncertain whether the pin can start at Z=0 and go up to Z=10mm based on these constraints.


A flat overhang at the wing knuckle's base at $Z = 2.5\text{ mm}$ presents a printing issue; a 45-degree conical slope is one solution. A 45°–53° conical retention surface could eliminate horizontal overhang entirely.

The goal is to design a Cylindrical Pin + Double-Conical Axial Retention structure where both the pin and knuckle bases sit at $Z = 0$ with no overhangs, radial clearance, and bidirectional axial retention. This seems feasible.


Analyzing pin connection methods given the wing's potential enclosure of the pin. Considering that the wing might not fully enclose the pin at all Z values, also noting possibilities where the pin connects at the bottom/top, the wing contains the pin, or the torso has an arm to the pin.

Exploring two topologies: one with a full 360° bore in the wing knuckle, and the other with a torso clevis/bridge connecting to the pin. Need to understand how the pin connects to the torso if the wing knuckle has a closed circular hole surrounding it in the middle layers. This could occur at the bottom or top of the joint.


If a torso arm supports the pin, the wing's Z-position above the arm is key during rotation. A wing knuckle passing over the arm creates an unsupported gap at Z=0 within the arm's angular sector, unless a bridge or conical frustum design is implemented to support the wing. The need for the bottom arm's existence is now in question given this observation.


The wing's limited swing angle, approximately ±30 degrees, changes joint design considerations. Need to determine if the bore encompasses the pin fully in the middle Z-layers or if there's torso-side pin connection at the top and bottom. Analyzing the joint in the XY-plane reveals the wing's outer and torso's inner boundaries relative to the rotation center.


Analyzing angular relationships: the wing's inner sector never intersects the wing stem.  Considering two joint configurations: full ring around the pin, or torso housing with wing-mounted pin. Need to compare which part carries the pin and which carries the bore, evaluating each option.


Re-evaluating the joint: either the torso holds the pin, or the wing does. Both configurations need careful examination, focusing on printability from Z=0 without supports.  Considering two cases: pin on the torso with a bore in the wing, or pin on the wing with a bore in the torso.

Assuming a pin centered at (Xj, Yj) with a 360-degree bore around it, and then at some height Z, how can both parts connect and touch the print bed at Z=0 without unsupported overhangs? Now working through a step-by-step tracing of this setup to check printability.


The pin, anchored at Z=0, presents a challenge for attachment to Part A, specifically if a connecting arm resides on the inner side. The arm's printability is questionable with Part B's 360-degree wrapping structure also resting at Z=0. Furthermore, how Part A's top arm could extend over Part B to connect to the pin at Z=7.6 mm needs a solution. The conflicting constraints require careful investigation of the arm's geometry.


A horizontal surface at Z=7.6 mm above a 0.6 mm gap presents an overhang issue for FDM printing. Printability constraints are now at odds with connecting Part A's top arm to the pin.

Two alternative configurations are under consideration: a 260° Part B with double-conical axial locking or a 360° Part B with 45° conical transitions, both aiming for no overhangs. Both configurations now require detailed analysis. Evaluating the 45° conical transition against the 260° C-knuckle and the 360° enclosed pin configurations is necessary.


The presence of a horizontal overhang suggests one part must cross over another in the Z-axis. Avoiding this requires that, at Z=0, parts either form a single connected region or merge upwards at a 45-degree angle or greater.

Considering the scenario of a pin within a 360-degree bore at Z=0, the pin forms an isolated island. To connect the pin to the torso without touching the surrounding bore, a non-overhanging connection method must be devised.


The pin-torso connection requires a bridge over a closed loop, necessitating a spanning bridge. This topology implies a spanning distance across the loop's width. Print-in-place bridging capability for the required span now needs investigation. The topological link suggests the span is unavoidable, presenting a potential printability issue.


Examining two pin-joint configurations: one with a torso clevis and the other with a partially enclosed pin by the wing. The clevis configuration requires careful Z-positioning of the wing knuckle to avoid interference with the bottom arm. A partially enclosed pin with a retaining cap and varying wing bore wrap angle (260° or 360°) presents an alternative. Determining the printability of each design based on the defined geometry and constraints is now critical.


Calculating the opening width of a partially wrapped bore shows that a 240-degree wrap allows radial escape. The formula confirms the bore's radial opening exceeds the pin diameter. This means the wing is not axially restrained if the bore is less than 360 degrees.


Calculated the angular constraint for a partially wrapped bore to ensure axial retention. Determined that a 240-degree wrap angle allows radial escape, leading to insufficient axial restraint. Derived the inequality for calculating the minimum wrap angle required to prevent radial escape. Concluded that a full 360-degree closed bore is necessary for robust XY retention in the current design, and a smaller wrap is not sufficient.


With the necessity of a full $360^\circ$ bore, axial retention strategies are limited.  Focus now shifts to how the pin connects to the torso *within* a closed bore.  The core question becomes finding a printable method for the pin to anchor at Z=0 while remaining enclosed by a full bore resting at Z=0, and withstanding axial forces.


Examining the configurations where either the torso or wing houses the $360^\circ$ pin, considering printability at Z=0. Evaluating two primary cases: torso-mounted pin and wing-mounted bore versus the reverse, with careful layer-by-layer tracing. The joint height, H_j = 12.0 mm, is within the Z limit, and the base structure for both parts will rest on Z=0.
  Tracing configurations that include: torso clevis with the wing center eye and a wing resting at Z=0, and then consider also the wing clevis and torso center eye designs. The approach will assess printability and axial retention for each variant.


Considering a pin that starts at Z=0 and extends upwards, it lacks overhang at its base. Similarly, if a ring structure (wing knuckle) also starts at Z=0 and surrounds the pin, both structures are directly on the build plate at Z=0.


Visualizing the described Z=0 configuration shows all parts flat on the print bed, confirming no initial overhangs.  Need to determine how axial locking in both +Z and -Z directions will occur for the wing, given this initial state. The challenge is ensuring retention without needing supports.


Examined the pin and bore radii, $R_{\text{pin}}(Z)$ and $R_{\text{bore}}(Z)$, from Z=0 to 10 mm to evaluate axial retention. Noticed a vertical skirt from Z=0 to 1mm, followed by an inward taper from Z=1mm to 2.5mm.  Calculated the taper as 45 degrees. Realized an inward taper on the pin doesn't cause an overhang.


The 45-degree inward taper of the bore is support-free for FDM printing. The pin's base radius, larger than the bore's inner radius at a certain Z-height, mechanically prevents downward wing movement. The central cylindrical section has a specified pin and bore radius, resulting in 0.5 mm radial clearance.


The top conical flare of the pin and bore provides a support-free axial lock, preventing upward wing movement relative to the pin. The pin flare's larger radius creates interference with the bore, generating a mechanical stop. The focus is now on connecting the pin to either the torso or the wing.


The Wing Knuckle ends at Z=8.0 mm, its top having a narrow 1.8 mm radial width. Considering the top, the outer wall could taper inward at 45 degrees, or the torso's bridge arch over the knuckle. At Z=8.0 mm, the pin's radius is less than or equal to 4.2 mm, while the torso wall is at least 7.0 mm.


Considering bridging the $2.8\text{ mm}$ gap between the pin and torso shoulder pillar using a $45^\circ$ arch to support the wing knuckle. Both pin and pillar are part of the torso and extend from Z=0 to Z=8.0 mm. The wing knuckle sits between them. A $45^\circ$ arch originating from both sides of the gap would span the distance, supporting the wing. The pin radius is $\le 4.2\text{ mm}$, the pillar radius is $\ge 7.0\text{ mm}$, and the wing's radial range is $4.7\text{ mm} \le r \le 6.5\text{ mm}$.


The pin and torso shoulder pillar are growing towards each other at 45 degrees, creating a $45^\circ$ arch where they meet. The geometry results in both having a 5.6 mm radius at a Z of 9.4 mm. The wing knuckle's top is roof-shaped, positioned below the arch, and exhibits a consistent clearance. I'll need to carefully verify this "45° Gothic-Arch Captive Hourglass Pin Joint" by tracing its cross-section.


Examining the design from Z=0 upwards, the pin, wing knuckle, torso shoulder, and wing blade all rest on the build plate. The pin and wing knuckle have a 0.5 mm radial clearance. A vertical skirt exists from Z=0 to 0.8 mm, followed by a 45-degree inward taper on the wing knuckle's bore. This design mechanically locks the wing in the Z- direction, and there are no overhangs. The goal now is to determine how the pin connects to the torso or wing.


Analyzing axial retention further, a 45-degree inward taper on both the pin and the wing knuckle's bore is found. This eliminates overhangs and provides mechanical locking. The horizontal radial clearance between the pin and bore remains consistent at 0.5 mm throughout the design. The central cylindrical region maintains the specified radial clearance, confirming the joint's function. Conical sections provide a support-free axial lock. The key now is the connection to the torso. The current model shows all features resting flat on the print bed.


A conical retention zone, with a 45-degree outward flare on both pin and bore, creates a 0.5 mm radial gap and requires no print supports. The pin radius increases from 2.7 mm to 4.0 mm, and the bore from 3.2 mm to 4.5 mm within the zone.

Analyzing the Gothic-Arch bridge, the wing knuckle spans from 4.5 mm to 6.9 mm at Z = 7.4 mm. The goal is to design this section's printability.


Analyzing the Torso Top Bridge connecting the pin and shoulder, both are expanding at 45 degrees towards a merged point.  Pin radius increases from 4.0 mm to 5.7 mm from Z=7.4 mm to Z=9.1 mm, while the shoulder radius decreases from 7.4 mm to 5.7 mm within the same range.  At Z=9.1 mm, the pin and shoulder fully merge at a radius of 5.7 mm.  This merged region needs careful verification regarding its impact on the wing knuckle.


The pin connects to the torso via a bridge from Z=9.1 mm to 11.8 mm, forming a solid structural link. All joint components (torso, pins, wings) rest flat on the print bed. Every transition features a 45-degree slope, eliminating the need for support structures. The bore fully encloses the pin from Z=0 to Z=8.2 mm.


The wing knuckle fully encloses the pin as a complete $360^\circ$ ring.  A precise 0.5 mm radial clearance is confirmed within the cylindrical sections of the pin and bore. This clearance remains consistent throughout the joint, including conical sections. The wing's downward axial movement is prevented because the bore radius is smaller than the pin's base radius.


The wing cannot move upwards due to two constraints: interference between the wing bore and pin at certain heights, and the torso's Gothic-Arch bridge physically blocking upward motion above the wing knuckle.

The pin's strength needs evaluation given that it only connects to the torso at the top. The pin is anchored to the build plate at Z=0, merging into the torso at Z=9.1 mm.


A top-connected pin design using a Gothic arch is structurally sound. A full, print-bed-resting $360^\circ$ wing knuckle is better. This configuration eliminates bridging issues at the bottom and ensures both pin and knuckle sit flat at Z=0. Furthermore, the arch's merging solid columns enhance the joint's robustness.


Considering increased pin diameter from 6 mm. Redefining pin and bore radii at the mid-shaft as 3.00 mm and 3.50 mm respectively, with 0.5 mm radial clearance. Also considering a larger pin flare and bore flare with radii of 4.30 mm and 4.80 mm respectively. Redefined knuckle radius at 7.20 mm, with torso clearance at 7.70 mm. The Gothic arch bridge dimensions were also reviewed with updated values.


Defined a layer-by-layer description of the pin and bore's dimensions from Z=0 to Z=2.1 mm, focusing on a 0.2 mm layer height. Calculated the radial clearance at 0.5 mm. Noted a 45° taper on the bottom conical retention zone.

From Z=0.0 to 0.8 mm (Layers 1-4), pin and bore are cylindrical, with respective radii of 4.30 mm and 4.80 mm, maintaining a 0.50 mm clearance. A wing knuckle radius of 7.20 mm and torso inner clearance radius of 7.70 mm were also noted.

From Z=0.8 mm to 2.1 mm, the radii taper at 45° within the bottom conical retention zone: pin radius decreases from 4.30 mm to 3.00 mm, and bore radius from 4.80 mm to 3.50 mm. The 0.50 mm radial clearance remains consistent.


The existing 45-degree conical design was re-evaluated, and a steeper 50.9-degree angle was explored to improve printability, noting this simplifies overhangs. Calculations confirmed the increased angle provides sufficient Z-clearance and radial clearance for successful printing without layer fusion. The middle cylindrical shaft and bore's Z transition heights will be aligned to multiples of the layer height.


Layer-by-layer joint geometry from Z=0 to 7.6 mm was traced using a 0.2 mm layer height.  A vertical skirt, conical retention zones, and a cylindrical pin and bore section were defined.  The bottom conical section transitions from cylindrical geometry to the 3.00 mm pin radius and 3.50 mm bore radius.

The cylindrical shaft section maintains a 0.50 mm radial clearance. The top conical retention zone tapers outward to establish a secure locking mechanism. Analysis continued with the wing knuckle from Z = 7.6 mm.


From Z=7.6 mm to Z=8.6 mm, the wing knuckle has inward and outward slopes, culminating in a flat top ring. Analyzing the torso's arch above this section, the pin and torso shoulder geometry are examined between Z=7.6 mm and Z=9.8 mm. I will now characterize the pin and torso shoulder flare. The pin expands outward, and the shoulder flares inward until the radii match. I need to verify that this is manufacturable.


Verified a seamless pin-torso shoulder connection at Z = 9.8 mm and r = 6.00 mm. Then checked clearance between the wing knuckle's top and torso arch at Z = 8.6 mm, calculating a vertical clearance of 0.68 mm to 1.20 mm. The radial clearance along the sloped sides is a consistent 0.50 mm. The torso shoulder bridge provides solid connection from Z = 9.8 to 12.6 mm, with a rounded dome.


Joint dimensions are reviewed, confirming consistent 0.50 mm radial clearance and favorable overhang angles across all sections. There are no bridges or overhangs below the critical angle.

Carefully tracing the joint geometry, specifically the torso shoulder's arching bridge and its relationship to the wing knuckle, is required. Need to confirm the specified radial and vertical clearances are maintained within the $110^\circ$ inner sector.


Considering pin and shoulder connection at heights $Z > 8.6\text{ mm}$, the pin extends to $Z = 12.6\text{ mm}$ with a $110^\circ$ Gothic-Arch Bridge. Investigating the wing blade, its height is from $Z = 0$ to $8.0\text{ mm}$, and the wing blade attaches to the wing knuckle's outer sector. Determining the wing's rotation clearance, given a wing blade angular width of $70^\circ$, requires calculating potential blade-to-torso wall interference.


The wing's rotation clearance depends on the torso shoulder, the wing blade's sector width and the wing stem's position. Angular interference must be calculated to establish the limits of wing articulation. Defining the angular sector of the wing blade and the torso's shoulder, and then deriving the angular rotation limit is required. Determining the allowable rotation angle, given torso and wing sectors, is critical.


Determining the wing's clearance during rotation requires a full kinematic analysis. Defining potential collision points necessitates precise mapping of wing points in the XY plane relative to the torso. Calculating the position of points on the wing as it swings through a defined range is the next step.


Analyzing wing kinematics, the goal is to prevent collisions between the left and right wings during rotation. Evaluating the wing's range of motion, from $-38^\circ$ to $+38^\circ$, is crucial. Ensuring that every point on the left wing maintains $Y > +0.5 \text{ mm}$ guarantees no collision with the symmetrical right wing, which stays at $Y < -0.5 \text{ mm}$. The wing-torso collision risks must also be evaluated.


If each wing's Y-coordinate is constrained relative to $Y = \pm 0.5$ mm, wing collisions are impossible. Defining the Left Wing's neutral pose coordinates using polar coordinates relative to the joint center, I can check this.

The negative Y direction is equivalent to a $\phi$ of $-90^\circ$, and outward is $+90^\circ$; forward is $0^\circ$, backward is $\pm 180^\circ$. A Torso profile check needs to occur.


Analyzing wing kinematics, the goal is to prevent collisions between the wing and torso during rotation, particularly within the defined angular range. The Torso's geometry near the joint must allow free wing movement. Torso half-width constrains the wing's range of motion, with joint centers at $(2.0, \pm 10.5)$ mm.

The clearance is calculated from the joint center to the midline Y=0 as $Y_j = 10.5$ mm. The torso's outer boundary near the joint is approximated by a circular arc of radius $R_{torso\_clear} = 7.70$ mm centered at the joint. Torso clearance near the joint is evaluated at radii greater than 7.20 mm. The wing's angular position relative to the torso is analyzed, focusing on the region where head and antennae are positioned. The critical angle, relative to the joint center, is determined, considering a 38-degree forward displacement from the negative Y-direction. Determining the head's geometry, with compound eyes and antennae, requires specifying their dimensions and print bed contact. Antennae must be wide enough to avoid breakage. Torso's segmented structure and dual joint shoulders are also defined.

Breaking down the design is necessary to ensure mechanical robustness and adherence to specifications. The goal is to produce a design that prints easily without supports, while also passing all relevant tests for geometry, kinematics, and slicer compatibility. Simultaneously, the design must achieve the artistic and recognizable appearance of a detailed butterfly.


Defining a coordinate system and establishing dimensional constraints is crucial for a printable and articulated butterfly model. A centered coordinate system with the X-axis representing the torso's length seems appropriate, placing the head at positive X and abdomen at negative X. The target total X-length of 96 mm stays well within the 120 mm dimension. Y-axis will represent wing span, and the model is symmetric across the XZ-plane.


Y-axis defines wing span, with the left wing at positive Y and right wing at negative Y, targeting a 92 mm total span (±46 mm). The Z-axis represents vertical height, with the model's base on the print bed at Z = 0; this means the torso and wings also rest on the build plate. This configuration ensures no unsupported overhangs during 3D printing. The maximum height is about 12 mm for the body and head, and 4-8 mm for the wings.


All model parts must rest on the print bed at Z = 0, eliminating any mid-air floating elements on the first layer. This needs careful consideration for joints requiring axial retention along the Z-axis.

A print-in-place vertical-axis pin joint can still function with parts resting at Z = 0, allowing for bidirectional axial retention. The design will now focus on the pin joint's construction and functionality to ensure both printability and axial retention.


Considering Z-axis pin joints, axial retention is crucial for print-in-place functionality. One approach uses a clevis/captive pin with a conical collar (double-cone or hourglass shape).

The other potential approach needs to be carefully investigated, considering the print-in-place constraints and axial retention requirements. Radial clearance between the pin and hole must be within 0.4-0.6 mm per side to ensure movement. All joint surfaces need non-zero gaps.


Considering a pin-type revolute joint, either the torso or the wing could contain the pin. Both configurations must be evaluated for printability. Case 1 assumes a torso-mounted captive pin and a wing-mounted bore. A pin-type joint consists of a cylindrical pin and a shaft hole with a radial clearance of 0.4-0.6 mm.


Ensuring true cylindrical sections for the pin and bore facilitates a consistent, predictable radial clearance as specified. The specified 0.4-0.6 mm single-side clearance translates directly to $c_{\text{radial}} = R_{\text{bore}} - R_{\text{pin}} = 0.50\text{ mm}$ (midpoint) in the joint cross-section.

The critical challenge now is implementing axial retention along the Z-axis without requiring any print supports or lifting parts off the build plate at Z=0. Exploring joint geometry in (r, Z) coordinates is the next step to achieve this.


The pin's connection to the torso requires careful consideration of axial retention and print-in-place constraints, specifically from Z=0 to Z=10mm. Two potential approaches are identified: a double-shear clevis pin configuration or a pin with conical retention flares. If a bottom arm supports the pin, the wing knuckle's Z-position must be evaluated to ensure proper articulation and prevent interference during printing. A flat overhang at the wing knuckle's base at $Z = 2.5\text{ mm}$ presents a printing issue; a 45-degree conical slope is one solution. A 45°–53° conical retention surface could eliminate horizontal overhang entirely.

Verified the part files, noting fixed torso, left wing (+Y), and right wing (-Y). Investigating the `joints.json` structure to ensure clarity for both automated evaluation and human review. The root fields will define the `fixed_part` (e.g., "parts/parts\_1.stl"), units ("mm"), and coordinate system with X as torso longitudinal.


Examining the data structure for joint articulation; specifically focusing on `"joints.json"` format requirements. Considering fields such as `id`, `type`, `parent`/`child` parts, rotation `axis`, `position`, and `range`. The different possible formats for defining the `range` is noted (array vs. object).

The `parts` array within `"joints.json"` will be used to define the model parts, including file paths to STL files. Further investigation of data format includes parts' `id`, `name`, `role`, `file`, and the fixed/moving status.


Verified that redundant "range" and "limits" keys in the joint objects do not violate JSON structure and ensure correct value access. Considered that creating output directories is the next step to store generated model files.
